title: What is Spark write-time partitioning (`df.write.partitionBy("country")`) — organizing data into directories by column values — and how does it enable partition pruning (queries filtering on the partition column skip irrelevant directories)?
shortTitle: Spark write-time partitioning (`df.write.partitionBy`) and partition pruning

s1_definition.profdef: Write-time partitioning instructs Spark to physically organize output files into a directory hierarchy keyed by the values of one or more columns, using `df.write.partitionBy("col")`. Each distinct value becomes a subdirectory, and the column itself is removed from the data files because its value is encoded in the path. When a later query filters on that partition column, Spark reads only the matching directories and skips the rest — this is partition pruning, and it dramatically reduces the amount of data scanned.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India stores transaction records in a giant filing room. Without partitioning, every record for every branch is dumped into one enormous drawer, and finding Mumbai's records means reading everything. Write-time partitioning is like labelling one drawer per branch: "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Chennai". Now when the auditor asks only for Mumbai, the clerk opens just the Mumbai drawer and ignores the rest. That skipping of irrelevant drawers is partition pruning.
s1_definition.oneliner: `partitionBy` writes data into value-named directories so queries filtering on that column read only the matching directories and skip everything else.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Write-time partitioning instructs Spark to physically organize output files into a directory hierarchy keyed by the values of one or more columns, using `df.write.partitionBy("col")`. Each distinct value becomes a subdirectory, and the column itself is removed from the data files because its value is encoded in the path. When a later query filters on that partition column, Spark reads only the matching directories and skips the rest — this is partition pruning, and it dramatically reduces the amount of data scanned.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India stores transaction records in a giant filing room. Without partitioning, every record for every branch is dumped into one enormous drawer, and finding Mumbai's records means reading everything. Write-time partitioning is like labelling one drawer per branch: "Mumbai", "Delhi", "Chennai". Now when the auditor asks only for Mumbai, the clerk opens just the Mumbai drawer and ignores the rest. That skipping of irrelevant drawers is partition pruning.

**One line to remember:** `partitionBy` writes data into value-named directories so queries filtering on that column read only the matching directories and skip everything else.

sections.s2_technical:
When you call `df.write.partitionBy("branch").parquet(path)`, Spark groups the rows by the branch value and writes each group into its own subdirectory named like `branch=Mumbai/`, `branch=Delhi/`, and so on. The partition column's value lives in the directory name, not inside the Parquet files, which also saves a little storage because the repeated value is not stored per row. This layout is sometimes called Hive-style partitioning because the `column=value` directory convention comes from Hive.

Partition pruning happens at read time. When you later run `spark.read.parquet(path).filter(col("branch") === "Mumbai")`, the Catalyst Optimizer recognizes that the filter is on a partition column. Instead of listing and reading every directory, it lists only `branch=Mumbai/` and feeds only those files into the scan. Everything else is skipped before a single row is read. This is the most powerful form of data skipping because it eliminates whole directories, not just rows — the I/O you save is enormous when the filter is selective.

You can partition by multiple columns, for example `partitionBy("branch", "txnDate")`, which creates a nested directory tree like `branch=Mumbai/txnDate=2026-10-30/`. A query filtering on both columns prunes at both levels. The order matters: the first column is the outer directory, so put the column you filter on most often, or the most selective one, first.

A senior-level nuance is cardinality. Partitioning works well for low-cardinality columns like branch or country, because each directory then holds a healthy amount of data. Partitioning on a high-cardinality column like account id or timestamp creates millions of tiny directories, which bloats metadata, causes the small-file problem, and can even make the driver run out of memory listing them. So you partition by columns with few distinct values that you frequently filter on, and you combine with bucketing or avoid partitioning for high-cardinality keys.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India stores years of transactions in the data lake. Analysts constantly run reports for a single branch, but every report scans the entire dataset because the files are unpartitioned, so a Mumbai report reads Delhi and Chennai data too. This is exactly what write-time partitioning fixes — writing with `partitionBy("branch")` puts each branch in its own directory.

Problem 2 — After partitioning, a query filtering on branch must actually skip the other branches, not just filter rows after reading them. This is partition pruning — Spark lists only the matching branch directory and never touches the others, so the scan reads a fraction of the data.

The demo models a directory layout keyed by branch, simulates a query filtered on one branch, and shows how many directories and bytes are skipped versus a full scan, logging the pruning decision.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four branch directories written by `partitionBy("branch")` — Mumbai (900 MB), Delhi (750 MB), Chennai (600 MB), Kolkata (550 MB).

Step 1: Without pruning, a query would scan all four directories, totalling 2800 MB. This is the baseline cost.

Step 2: The query filters on `branch = 'Mumbai'`. The pruner recognizes the filter is on the partition column, so it keeps only the `branch=Mumbai` directory.

Step 3: The pruned scan reads just 900 MB from one directory. Three directories and 1900 MB are skipped entirely — not filtered after reading, but never read at all.

Step 4: The demo logs the full-scan size, the pruned-scan size, the number of skipped directories, and the bytes saved, then logs that it reads only the Mumbai directory.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 04:25:12 [INFO] Full scan (no pruning): 2800 MB across 4 directories
2026-10-30 04:25:12 [INFO] Pruned scan (branch=Mumbai): 900 MB across 1 directory
2026-10-30 04:25:12 [INFO] Directories skipped: 3, bytes saved: 1900 MB
2026-10-30 04:25:12 [INFO] Partition pruning read only the Mumbai directory and skipped the rest.
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  WRITE:  df.write.partitionBy("branch")
    │
    ▼
  s3://bank/txns/
    ├── branch=Mumbai/   (900 MB)
    ├── branch=Delhi/    (750 MB)
    ├── branch=Chennai/  (600 MB)
    └── branch=Kolkata/  (550 MB)

  READ:   filter(branch = 'Mumbai')
    │ Catalyst sees filter on partition column
    ▼
  LIST only branch=Mumbai/    ← prune
    ├─ skip branch=Delhi/   ✗
    ├─ skip branch=Chennai/ ✗
    └─ skip branch=Kolkata/ ✗
    ▼
  Scan 900 MB (not 2800 MB)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Write-time partitioning organizes the output physically into a directory hierarchy keyed by a column's values. When I call write with partitionBy on the branch column, Spark creates one subdirectory per branch, named like branch equals Mumbai, and it moves the column's value into the directory name rather than storing it in every file. This follows the Hive-style convention of column-equals-value directories.

The payoff comes at read time through partition pruning. When a later query filters on the partition column, the Catalyst Optimizer recognizes that the filter matches the directory structure, so instead of listing and reading every directory it lists only the matching ones and skips the rest entirely. The important point is that this is data skipping at the directory level — the irrelevant data is never read at all, not read and then filtered. That is why pruning is so powerful: a selective filter on a partition column can turn a multi-terabyte scan into a few gigabytes.

In my work at the National Bank of India the transaction lake was partitioned by branch and date, so analysts querying a single branch for a single day touched only that one small directory instead of years of data across all branches. The one caution I always raise is cardinality. Partitioning shines on low-cardinality columns like branch or country where each directory holds a healthy amount of data. If you partition on a high-cardinality column like account id, you create millions of tiny directories, which bloats metadata, triggers the small-file problem, and can even crash the driver while listing them. So my rule is: partition by low-cardinality columns you filter on frequently, order the most-filtered column first, and reach for bucketing instead when the key is high-cardinality.
